questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what urbanization measures
questions.stem: In a chef's costing sheet for a city-centre kitchen, one line records how many of the city's residents now live in urban areas. What does urbanization describe?

options.text: The number of people who leave the countryside each year to take jobs in city restaurants and hotels
options.misconception: treats urbanization as only the flow of rural migrants

options.text: The share of a population living in urban areas, together with the movement of people into them
The proportion of urban workers employed in catering, hospitality, and food service businesses
options.misconception: restricts urbanization to work in the catering sector

options.text: The speed at which a single city's boundary expands and turns farmland into built plots
options.misconception: confuses urbanization with a city's physical sprawl

questions.explanation: Urbanization is the proportion of people living in urban areas plus the movement of people into them. A single-year count of migrants and a city's boundary growth describe other processes entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what share of people live in towns, not how many arrive.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Separate urban growth rate from the urbanization level
questions.stem: A regional costing sheet shows the urban share of population rising from 41 to 44 per cent in eleven years while the city population grows from 0.82 million to 1.05 million. What does the urban growth rate of about 2.3 per cent a year tell you?

options.text: That the region has become fully urban, since a 2.3 per cent rate adds up quickly
options.misconception: treats a modest growth rate as if the region were fully urban

options.text: That most of the city's growth came from rural villagers moving into the built-up area
options.misconception: assumes all urban growth is rural-to-urban migration

options.text: That the urban share of the population must have risen by 2.3 percentage points each year
options.misconception: confuses a growth rate with a change in population share

options.text: That the urban population is expanding at about 2.3 per cent a year, which is a rate rather than a level

questions.explanation: A growth rate says how fast a population rises each year, not how urban a region already is. The 41 to 44 per cent figures are the level of urbanization; 2.3 per cent is the pace of growth.
questions.hint: A rate measures change over time, the level measures position.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate an average annual urban growth rate
questions.stem: A chef's costing sheet shows that the town supplying the kitchen grew from 120,000 residents in 2005 to 150,000 in 2020. Explain how you would calculate the average annual urban growth rate for those fifteen years and what the result means.

answer.exemplar: Compute the ratio 150,000 to 120,000, which is 1.25, then take the fifteenth root to get about 1.015 times per year, giving an average annual growth rate of roughly 1.5 per cent. This describes the pace of increase in the urban population over the period and can be compared with rates elsewhere.

questions.explanation: Annual growth rate smooths change across the period into a yearly percentage, so towns of different sizes can be compared. It is compounded, not a simple average of yearly changes.
questions.hint: Divide by the years elapsed, not by the start figure.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate net rural-to-urban migration
questions.stem: A costing sheet for a district records 240,000 residents in 2000 and 300,000 in 2020. Natural increase over the same period was 45,000. How many people moved from rural areas into the district's towns?
questions.explanation: Growth of 60,000 came from 45,000 of natural increase plus the balance from migration. Subtracting natural increase isolates the net movement of people into the towns.
questions.hint: Total change minus natural increase gives net migration.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Justify enumeration over sampling

stimulus.body: The head chef asks the costing clerk to record every delivery of flour to the district's kitchens for one full year, including deliveries to the single village bakery. The clerk notes that some small shops buy from traders rather than from any recorded supplier.

questions.stem: The clerk has to count the people and trade in the district. Which approach, and why, does the note support?

options.text: Sample twenty bakeries and multiply up, because a full count would take longer than the budget allows
options.misconception: assumes a sample scaled up is as reliable as a complete count

options.text: Survey only the district's registered catering businesses, because informal traders are not part of the economy
options.misconception: believes only registered businesses count as economic activity

options.text: Enumerate every household and trader, because only a full count shows every group including informal sellers
Survey the market on one busy Saturday, because market day reveals typical trading patterns for the week
options.misconception: treats one busy market day as representative of the whole year

questions.explanation: Enumeration counts every unit, so no group is missed and small groups can still be reported. A scaled-up sample keeps the error of its chosen sites, and one market day reflects only itself.
questions.hint: Ask which method would leave no group uncounted.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a census year must be recorded
questions.stem: Two kitchens compare their covers served: one count came from a census year and one from a later household survey. First identify why the census year is recorded, then choose the effect on a comparison.

options.text: Census figures describe a single year, so comparisons must match years or adjust for change first
Census years matter only for tax purposes, so demographic comparison between years is always safe
options.misconception: believes the census year has no bearing on comparability

options.text: Because the census is a single snapshot, it can never be compared with a survey from any other year
options.misconception: claims no census figure can ever be compared with a survey

options.text: Older census years are always wrong and should be discarded whenever newer data exist
options.misconception: assumes the most recent count always makes older counts useless

questions.explanation: A census is a snapshot of a named year, and populations, boundaries, and prices shift between counts. Comparing years is legitimate only when the differences in year and coverage are stated or adjusted for.
questions.hint: Ask which year the snapshot belongs to before comparing.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Checking a census against a survey
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a gap between a census and a survey
questions.stem: A cost sheet shows census counts and a separate household survey for the same district, and the two disagree by four per cent. Which check is the most useful?

options.text: Discard the survey immediately, because a census is always more accurate than any sample-based estimate
options.misconception: assumes census counts are error free by definition

options.text: Average the two figures, because the midpoint of two counts must be closer to the truth
options.misconception: believes averaging two disagreeing figures reduces the error

options.text: Assume the census is wrong, because a survey that visits every home would be harder to falsify
options.misconception: assumes only a full survey can ever be trusted

options.text: Compare the two sets by age, sex, and area to find which groups they disagree about

questions.explanation: The disagreement itself is the clue, and comparing by age, sex, and area shows where it lies. Averaging hides the problem, and a four per cent gap does not condemn either source.
questions.hint: Find where the two sources differ, not just that they do.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Derive urban population from a share
questions.stem: A costing sheet for a chain of four city kitchens shows that in 1995 the district had 55 per cent of its people in urban areas and 300,000 residents; by 2025 the urban share is 70 per cent with 480,000 residents. Which reading is correct?

options.text: The urban share rose 15 percentage points, so most of the new residents must have come from other districts
options.misconception: confuses a change in share with the origin of new residents

options.text: The urban share rose 15 percentage points and the urban population grew from 165,000 to 336,000
The urban share of 70 per cent means 336,000 people moved in from the countryside
options.misconception: assumes every addition to the urban population is a rural migrant

options.text: Since total population grew by 60 per cent, the urban share could not have risen at all
options.misconception: believes faster total growth must mean a smaller urban share

questions.explanation: Applying each share to its total gives 165,000 urban residents in 1995 and 336,000 in 2025, so the urban population more than doubled. The share rise alone cannot show where the new residents came from.
questions.hint: Multiply each percentage by the population it applies to.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish growth rate from urban share
questions.stem: A regional kitchen's costing sheet shows the urban share of population rising from 38 to 52 per cent between 1990 and 2020. Explain why the urban share rising and the urban growth rate rising are different facts, and give a case where one rose while the other did not.

answer.exemplar: The urban share is a proportion of the whole population, so it can rise even when the urban population grows slowly if the rural population shrinks faster. The urban growth rate is the yearly pace at which the urban population itself expands. A mining town whose rural hinterland empties can gain urban share while its urban population grows at only one per cent a year.

questions.explanation: The share depends on the rural population too, so it can climb without fast urban growth. The rate describes only the urban population's pace, so the two can diverge.
questions.hint: A share depends on two populations; a rate depends on one.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Compute a simple average annual growth rate
questions.stem: A costing sheet for a city kitchen shows the district's urban population at 45,000 in 2010 and 63,000 in 2020. Using total percentage change divided by years, what is the average annual urban growth rate over that period?
questions.explanation: Change of 18,000 on a base of 45,000 is 40 per cent over ten years, giving an average annual rate of 4 per cent. The simple average sits above the compounded pace of about 3.4 per cent.
questions.hint: Take total percentage change, then divide by the years.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Infer net migration from two counts

stimulus.body: A village kitchen cooperative in the hills has lost most of its young cooks to the city kitchens. The treasurer records that the village had 2,400 residents at the last full count and about 1,900 at the most recent household survey, and that eleven births and four deaths were recorded between the two dates.

questions.stem: Using the treasurer's record, which conclusion about rural-to-urban migration in the village is best supported?

options.text: The village lost about 7 people net, since a fall of 500 minus natural increase of 7 leaves 493 leaving
The village gained population, because births always outnumber departures in farming settlements
options.misconception: assumes natural increase always exceeds out-migration in rural areas

options.text: About 500 people left, because a difference between a count and a survey measures migration only
options.misconception: treats any gap between a count and a survey as pure migration

options.text: No one left, because the gap between the count and the survey is small enough to ignore
options.misconception: dismisses a large discrepancy as too small to matter

questions.explanation: The fall of 500 must have the natural increase of seven removed, leaving a net loss of about 493 by migration. A gap between two sources is never pure migration, since timing and coverage also differ.
questions.hint: Remove natural increase before calling the gap migration.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Choose enumeration or sampling for a small area
questions.stem: A chain must decide how to count the households behind every delivery invoice. First identify what a complete count would settle that a sample cannot, then choose the better method for a small district.

options.text: Sample the largest customers, because large accounts make up most of the value of any delivery run
options.misconception: assumes the largest accounts represent the whole delivery network

options.text: Sample one street per district, because one street usually mirrors the habits of the whole town
options.misconception: assumes one street is representative of every household

options.text: Enumerate every household, because only a full count can report small groups and total value exactly
Skip counting entirely, because supplier invoices already record every sale that matters
options.misconception: assumes invoice records already replace an official population count

questions.explanation: A complete count has no sampling error and can publish figures for small areas and groups, which a scaled sample cannot guarantee. Samples remain useful for quick estimates but not for exact totals.
questions.hint: Ask what only a complete count can guarantee.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the census year
questions.stem: A city kitchen's costing sheet cites population figures for 1998 and again for 2023 in the same note. Why must the year of a census be recorded alongside its figures?

options.text: Because older counts were taken with slower methods and are therefore always wrong
options.misconception: assumes older methods make older counts entirely worthless

options.text: Because the year is needed only to work out how many years the kitchen has traded
options.misconception: believes the census year only matters for trading history

options.text: Because a census is a snapshot of one year, and populations and boundaries change over time
Because only counts taken in the present decade may be used in any costing work
options.misconception: believes only very recent counts may ever be cited

questions.explanation: A census describes one year, and population, boundaries, and urban definitions may all change afterwards. Recording the year lets readers judge whether two figures can be compared.
questions.hint: Ask what the snapshot could not have included.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Checking a census against a survey
questions.learningObjective: Explain a difference in average household size
questions.stem: A catering analyst compares a full count for a district with a survey of 200 households and finds the survey's average household size is 2.8 while the count implies 3.5. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: The survey may have missed larger or multi-person households, so the count is the safer base for totals
The survey is better, because a smaller sample always gives a more reliable average than a full count
options.misconception: believes a smaller sample always produces a more reliable average

options.text: The difference proves the survey was falsified deliberately by the households it visited
options.misconception: jumps to deliberate falsification from a size discrepancy

options.text: Both are equally valid, so the analyst should simply average the two household sizes together
options.misconception: thinks averaging disagreeing figures removes the disagreement

questions.explanation: A survey of 200 households can under-cover large or crowded homes, biasing average size down. The full count covers every household, so it is the sound basis for population totals.
questions.hint: Consider which households a small sample might skip.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret urban share alongside employer data
questions.stem: A hotel group's costing sheet notes that the chain's four city kitchens now prepare meals for a workforce of 900, and that 62 per cent of the district's residents now live in urban areas, up from 48 per cent in 1990. Explain what this combination of figures does and does not tell you about urbanization in the district.

answer.exemplar: The rising urban share shows that the district is urbanizing: a larger proportion of its residents live in towns and cities than in 1990. It does not reveal how much of the change came from rural-to-urban migration versus natural increase, nor whether the change is fast or slow for the region. The kitchen workforce figure describes one employer, not the destination of new arrivals.

questions.explanation: The urban share measures how urban the district is, but not the pace of change or its cause. Workforce numbers for one employer describe employment patterns, not population movement into the area.
questions.hint: Separate what is measured from what is only suggested.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Choose the correct base for a growth rate

stimulus.body: Kitchen handover notes record that the town's covered market had 22 stalls in 1995 and 31 stalls in 2015. The note states that the town's own population was 410,000 in 1995 and 480,000 in 2015.

questions.stem: Using the handover note, which calculation gives the average annual urban growth rate for the town between 1995 and 2015?

options.text: Adding 31 to 22, dividing by 20, because stalls are a direct measure of urban population
options.misconception: treats a market stall count as the town's population

options.text: Comparing 480,000 with 410,000 over 20 years, because population is the measure the rate describes
Dividing the rise in stalls by the rise in population, because stall growth matches population growth
options.misconception: assumes stall numbers track population numbers in a fixed ratio

options.text: Using the number of stalls only, because stall counts are always used to size urban areas
options.misconception: believes stall counts can substitute for a population denominator

questions.explanation: The rate describes how fast a population changes, so the town total is the right base. Stall numbers track trading activity, which can grow faster or slower than the people living there.
questions.hint: Choose the figure that the rate is supposed to describe.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Separate migration from natural change
questions.stem: A regional food hall's costing sheet shows the number of residents in the surrounding rural district falling from 58,000 to 49,000 in 12 years, with natural increase of 4,000. First work out the balance, then choose what it indicates about rural-to-urban migration.

options.text: The district gained about 5,000 people, because a smaller population with natural growth means net gain
options.misconception: ignores natural increase and reads a fall as a gain

options.text: The district lost about 9,000 people, because the fall in total population is the migration figure
options.misconception: uses the total population change and ignores natural increase

options.text: Nothing can be concluded, because rural-to-urban migration can never be separated from natural change
options.misconception: believes migration can never be separated from natural change

options.text: The district lost about 13,000 people by migration, once natural increase of 4,000 is removed

questions.explanation: The population fell by 9,000 while natural increase added 4,000, so migration removed about 13,000 people. Total change alone understates movement, because births and deaths partly offset it.
questions.hint: Natural change and movement push the total in different ways.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Justify a full count for ward figures
questions.stem: A city kitchen chain needs the number of meals served per day in every ward. Why is a full count preferred to a sample of twenty streets?

options.text: A full count gives every ward its own figure, so small wards are not hidden inside a regional average
A full count is preferred because sampling equipment in kitchens is expensive to hire
options.misconception: gives an equipment-cost reason for a statistical choice

options.text: A full count always takes less time than visiting twenty streets and counting every meal
options.misconception: assumes a complete count is automatically the quicker method

options.text: A sample is preferred instead, because twenty streets can be visited more often through the year
options.misconception: claims a small sample beats a full count on ward totals

questions.explanation: The advantage of enumeration is completeness, so each ward gets its own figure and small areas are not averaged away. A sample can miss quiet wards, and its cost says nothing about accuracy.
questions.hint: Think about which wards a small sample might overlook.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Report growth from two different sources
questions.stem: A city kitchen's analyst quotes a population count from 1996 and a household survey from 2021 for the same city, and finds the city has grown from 700,000 to 980,000. What must the analyst do with these two figures?

options.text: Treat them as directly comparable, because both count people living in the same city
options.misconception: assumes two counts are comparable without checking years

options.text: Discard the 1996 figure, because figures more than ten years old carry no information at all
options.misconception: believes old counts carry no useful information at all

options.text: Report the change with both years stated, because the interval includes both growth and boundary change
Average them into a single figure, because averaging removes the need to reconcile the two
options.misconception: thinks averaging disagreeing figures removes the disagreement

questions.explanation: A 1996 count and a 2021 survey are twenty-five years and maybe two boundary sets apart, so growth must be stated with both years. Averaging two totals destroys the change being measured.
questions.hint: State the year before you state the change.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Checking a census against a survey
questions.learningObjective: Sequence checks on conflicting estimates
questions.stem: A regional food-processing group finds its census-based sales forecast is 12 per cent below the figure produced by a household survey of 1,000 households. Explain a sensible sequence of checks before the group changes its forecasts.

answer.exemplar: The group should first confirm that the survey and the census used the same boundaries, the same definition of a household, and the same reference year, since any mismatch alone could explain much of the gap. It should then compare the two sources by age, sex, and area to find which groups drive the difference, and check the survey's response rate and whether hard-to-reach households were visited.

questions.explanation: Most gaps between sources come from coverage, definitions, or timing rather than error, so check those first. Comparing by group then shows whether the gap is concentrated or spread widely.
questions.hint: Check coverage, definitions, and timing before blaming error.

Total change of 60 per cent, and an average of 3 per cent a year, because 60,000 is 60 per cent

questions.learningObjective: Interpret balanced migration flows
questions.stem: A city's costing sheet records that arrivals of rural workers now equal departures of city workers each year. What does this tell you about rural-to-urban migration?

options.text: That rural-to-urban migration has stopped, because the two flows now cancel each other out
options.misconception: assumes equal inward and outward flows mean no movement

options.text: Nothing conclusive, because a balanced flow can hide heavy movement in both directions at once
That the city must be shrinking, because net arrivals and departures are the same each year
options.misconception: assumes a balanced flow implies the city population must fall

options.text: That every rural worker arriving must be settling permanently in the built-up area
options.misconception: assumes every arrival is a permanent settlement in the city

questions.learningObjective: Explain a gap between survey and full count
questions.stem: A catering survey of 400 diners in one market hall produced a mean spend of 14.50 per head. A separate full count of the hall's receipts gave a mean of 11.20 per head. What best explains the difference?

options.misconception: assumes the larger sample must be the more accurate one

options.text: The full count must be wrong, because it counted every customer and should match the survey
options.misconception: assumes a full count is automatically matched by any sample

options.text: Both are correct, because two different samples always produce two different means
options.misconception: treats a systematic difference as though it were random noise

questions.learningObjective: State growth with its years and interval
questions.stem: A city kitchen's analyst must report growth since 2001 but only has a 2019 survey and a 2024 count. Explain what a responsible statement of growth should say about the year and the interval.

answer.exemplar: The statement should name the two years, 2019 and 2024, and say that the growth figure covers five years rather than twenty-three. questions.explanation: Naming the years and the interval stops a five-year change being read as a long-run trend. Flagging the method difference keeps the survey-to-census comparison honest.

questions.stem: A census counted 1,200 households in a district and found 132 private cars. A survey of 150 households found that 14 per 100 households own a car. Applying the survey rate to all 1,200 households, how many more cars does it suggest than the census count?

options.text: Urbanization is not occurring, since the resident population of the districts has not changed

options.text: Urbanization is occurring through commuting, as people work in the city while living outside it
Urbanization is measured by the number of commuters, which is the only valid measure of the process

questions.explanation: Urbanization includes movement toward cities even when people keep a home outside the boundary, so commuting flows count. Resident numbers can stay flat while the city absorbs daily workers.

questions.explanation: The share rises while the total falls, so rural population is shrinking faster than urban population. Urbanization can therefore proceed with little absolute urban growth.

questions.stem: A city restaurant group's director asks why the group cannot use a sample of a thousand diners to work out the group's own total sales, even though the sample would be faster and cheaper. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A thousand diners describe the diners in the sample, not the diners who never chose the group's venue that year. Scaling a sample up assumes those unobserved diners behave like the observed ones, and any busy weekend or special event in the sample would inflate the group's estimate. For total sales the group needs every transaction, which is what a full record of the till provides.

questions.explanation: A scaled sample assumes unobserved customers behave like the ones observed, and a busy short period breaks that. Recording every transaction removes the assumption entirely for totals.
questions.hint: Ask what a sample of diners leaves out.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a compound growth pattern
questions.stem: A district's costing sheet gives urban population of 250,000 in 2000, 281,250 in 2010, and 316,406 in 2020. Explain what pattern these figures follow and what the average annual growth rate is.

answer.exemplar: Each figure is the previous one multiplied by 1.125, so the urban population grows by 12.5 per cent every ten years, which is a compound annual rate of about 2.5 per cent. The pattern is exponential rather than a constant addition, so an average annual growth rate describes it exactly here, and the same rate applies to every decade of the series.

questions.explanation: A constant percentage increase produces a curved series, so each decadal figure is the previous one multiplied by the same factor. That makes a single average annual rate a complete description of the trend shown here.
questions.hint: Look for a constant multiplier between decades.

questions.explanation: A per-resident cost combines a budget with a population count, and both shift over time. Naming the year tells the reader which pair was divided, so the comparison can be judged fairly.
questions.hint: Ask which two figures were divided by each other.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Checking a census against a survey
questions.learningObjective: Scale two rates and find the difference
questions.stem: A catering analyst puts a full count of 12,000 households in a district beside a survey of 300 households. The survey found 24 per cent had no internet access; the count implied 8 per cent. Applying the survey rate to the district, how many more households would be without access than the count suggests?

options.text: 960 households, because the count's own rate already gives the number without access
options.misconception: reads the count's rate as the answer to a difference question

options.text: 1,920 households, because 24 per cent of 12,000 is 2,880 and 8 per cent is 960
2,880 households, because the survey rate applied to all households is the difference
options.misconception: reports the survey estimate instead of the difference

options.text: 2,160 households, because the gap of 16 per cent applies to the 300 surveyed households
options.misconception: applies the rate gap to the sample rather than the district

questions.explanation: The survey rate applied to 12,000 households gives 2,880 without access, while the count implies 960, a difference of 1,920. The gap reflects coverage differences worth investigating.
questions.hint: Scale both rates to the whole district, then subtract.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain urbanization alongside rural decline
questions.stem: A county council's costing sheet records that the share of residents living in towns rose from 52 to 69 per cent while the county's rural population fell by nearly a third. Explain what that combination suggests about how urbanization happened there.

answer.exemplar: A rising urban share alongside a sharply shrinking rural population suggests that much of the urbanization came from rural residents moving into the towns of the same county, rather than from new residents arriving from outside. Natural increase in the towns would raise the share too, but it could not by itself account for a rural loss of a third in the same period.

questions.explanation: If the rural population fell sharply while the urban share rose, out-migration into the county's own towns is the most likely explanation, since natural increase alone would not empty the countryside.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to leave the countryside.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Compute an urban growth rate and its share
questions.stem: A region's costing sheet shows urban population of 180,000 in 2010 and 216,000 in 2020. It also shows the total population rising from 300,000 to 360,000. What was the average annual urban growth rate over the ten years, using total percentage change divided by years?
questions.explanation: Urban population grew 36,000 on a base of 180,000, which is 20 per cent over ten years, so 2 per cent a year. The urban share stayed at 60 per cent, so growth did not make the district more urban.
questions.hint: Base growth on the urban population, then divide by the years.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Compute an average annual growth rate

stimulus.body: A market hall's note records that the town held 12 permanent stalls in 2000 and 18 in 2020. A separate line records the town's population over the same period as 90,000 and 108,000.

questions.stem: Using the market note, what is the average annual growth rate of the town's population between 2000 and 2020?

options.text: 1 per cent a year, because the population grew 20 per cent over the twenty years
6 per cent a year, because the number of stalls rose by six over the twenty years
options.misconception: uses the stall count as a proxy for the population

options.text: 20 per cent a year, because the population rose by 20 per cent across the period
options.misconception: reports the total percentage change as the annual rate

options.text: 2 per cent a year, because the total rise of 18,000 should be doubled to get a rate
options.misconception: mangles the division by years and doubles the result

questions.explanation: The population rose 18,000 on a base of 90,000, which is 20 per cent over twenty years, so the annual rate is 1 per cent. Stall counts track trading, and a total percentage change is not a yearly rate.
questions.hint: Total percentage change, then divide by the years.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Work out urban population under total decline
questions.stem: A county's costing sheet shows the urban share of residents rising from 44 to 58 per cent while the total county population falls from 520,000 to 460,000. First work out what is happening to the urban population, then choose the correct reading.

options.text: The urban population must have fallen, because the county's total population fell by 60,000
options.misconception: assumes the urban population must follow the total population

options.text: No urbanization has occurred, because the county is losing people faster than towns are gaining them
options.misconception: confuses total population decline with absent urbanization

options.text: The urban population rose from 228,800 to 266,800, so urbanization continued despite county-wide decline
The urban population rose, but only because the county redefined which settlements count as urban
options.misconception: invokes a boundary redefinition without any evidence

questions.explanation: Applying the shares gives 228,800 urban residents in the first year and 266,800 in the second, so urban population grew even as the county lost people. Rural areas therefore shrank faster.
questions.hint: Multiply each urban share by its own year's population.
